name: Texture and Appearance Representation
text:
# Texture and Appearance Representation

Also called: Appearance Modeling, View-Dependent Rendering

## Overview
Texture and Appearance Representation defines how the color $c_i$ of a 3D Gaussian primitive is determined during rendering, extending the basic geometric parameters ($\boldsymbol{\mu}_i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i$) and opacity $\alpha_i$ [S1]. It solves the limitation of static color storage by enabling high-frequency details or view-dependent effects (specular highlights, anisotropy) without excessively increasing the number of primitives [S1]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [GaussianSet Data Structure](2074-gaussianset-data-structure.md) by focusing on the semantic definition of color rather than memory layout, and from [Primitive Geometry and Distribution](6228-primitive-geometry-and-distribution.md) by addressing radiance rather than shape [G].

## Shared principles
All child methods extend the standard 3D Gaussian primitive $i$ with additional appearance attributes $\mathbf{a}_i$ beyond the geometric parameters and opacity $\alpha_i$ [G]. The rendering pipeline retains the [front-to-back alpha-blending](#1141-front-to-back-compositing-unpremultiplied.md) equation, but the color contribution $c_i$ of each Gaussian is no longer a static vector. Instead, $c_i$ is computed by evaluating an appearance function that queries $\mathbf{a}_i$ using the viewing direction $\mathbf{v}$, surface normal $\mathbf{n}$, or local UV coordinates $\mathbf{u}_i$ [S1]. The final pixel color is calculated as:

$$
C(p) = \sum_{i \in \text{sorted}} c_i(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{a}_i) \alpha_i \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha_j)
$$

where $c_i$ is the color contribution derived from the specific appearance representation [S1]. This approach involves a trade-off between storage bandwidth, computational cost during decoding, and the complexity of the appearance being modeled [S1].

## Subtopics

### [Textured Gaussians](8061-textured-gaussians.md)
[Textured Gaussians](#8061-textured-gaussians.md) replace the standard spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients used for view-dependent color in 3D Gaussian [Splatting](#23-splatting.md) with explicit 2D textures mapped onto each primitive. This method solves the limitation of SH representations in capturing high-frequency appearance details without requiring an increase in the number of primitives. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [View-Dependent Appearance Representations](#14602-view-dependent-appearance-representations.md) by utilizing spatial UV sampling rather than directional basis functions, enabling high-fidelity texture reconstruction. See [Textured Gaussians](8061-textured-gaussians.md).

### [View-Dependent Appearance Representations](14602-view-dependent-appearance-representations.md)
This family of methods extends the standard 3D Gaussian primitive with appearance attributes $\mathbf{a}_i$ to model view-dependent color $c_i(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{a}_i)$, where $\mathbf{v}$ is the viewing direction. Unlike static color storage, these representations decode color dynamically based on the viewing angle, enabling the modeling of specular highlights, anisotropy, and complex lighting effects. The rendering pipeline retains front-to-back [alpha-blending](#5750-alpha-blending.md), but the color contribution of each Gaussian is computed via an appearance function that queries $\mathbf{a}_i$ using $\mathbf{v}$, surface normal $\mathbf{n}$, or local coordinates. This approach trades off storage bandwidth, decoding computational cost, and representation complexity. See [View-Dependent Appearance Representations](14602-view-dependent-appearance-representations.md).

#### View-Dependent Gaussian Splatting
Models 3DGS to represent 3D shapes and predicts attributes like view-dependent color and opacity using a NeRF-like neural network, replacing the Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients used in [original 3DGS](#2805-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-software.md) [S1].

#### Neural BRDF for 3D Gaussian Splatting
Simplifies the [BRDF](#14809-bidirectional-reflectance-distribution-function-brdf.md) to a neural shader that predicts specular and diffuse components directly from the view direction and a learnable material feature [S2, unofficial].

#### Neural Texture Splatting
Encodes textures as small neural networks evaluated at Gaussian coordinates, which can be deformed to model dynamic appearances and fine geometric displacements [S2, unofficial].

## Background
The standard [3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)](#1174-3d-gaussian-splatting-3dgs.md) method originally used [Spherical Harmonics](#5603-spherical-harmonics.md) (SH) to represent view-dependent color [S1]. However, SH has limitations in capturing high-frequency details and complex lighting effects [S1]. Recent advances introduced explicit 2D textures and neural appearance models to overcome these limitations [S1][S2, unofficial]. View-Dependent Gaussian Splatting (VDGS) proposed using NeRF-like networks to predict view-dependent attributes [S1]. [Neural Texture](#16067-neural-textures.md) Splatting extended this by encoding textures as neural networks [S2, unofficial]. These methods aim to improve visual fidelity while maintaining the real-time performance of Gaussian splatting [S1][S2, unofficial].

## Sources
